# Imaging Apparatus, Image Sensor, and Image Processor for Reduced Processing Load

## Background and Overview

The present disclosure relates to an imaging apparatus, an image sensor, and an image processor that collectively address a persistent challenge in modern imaging systems: the substantial computational burden placed on image processing units during image recognition operations. As imaging applications increasingly demand real-time recognition capabilities—such as face detection, object tracking, and scene analysis—the processing load on downstream image processing units has grown significantly, often creating bottlenecks that limit overall system performance and responsiveness.

## Image Sensor Architecture and Functionality

At the core of this disclosure is an image sensor equipped with a plurality of photoelectric conversion elements arranged in a grid pattern, extending both vertically and horizontally across the imaging surface. Each of these elements performs photoelectric conversion, transforming incident light into corresponding pixel signals. The aggregate of these pixel signals constitutes the image data output by the sensor, representing a complete captured frame.

A distinguishing feature of this image sensor lies in its structural organization: the imaging surface is not treated as a single, undifferentiated plane but is instead partitioned into multiple discrete areas. This areal division enables the sensor to perform localized analysis rather than relying solely on whole-frame processing performed downstream.

## Generation of Image Recognition Support Information

For each of these defined areas, the image sensor independently generates image recognition support information. This information is derived directly from the pixel signals generated by the photoelectric conversion elements located within that specific area. By performing this area-based analysis at the sensor level—prior to or in parallel with the transmission of full image data—the sensor effectively pre-processes portions of the visual information that would otherwise need to be computed entirely by the image processing unit.

This support information serves as a form of preliminary or auxiliary data that characterizes relevant features within each area, potentially including indicators related to brightness distribution, edge characteristics, motion, or other attributes pertinent to recognition tasks. Because this information is generated on an area-by-area basis, it provides spatially localized insight into the image content, which can be leveraged to guide or accelerate subsequent recognition processes.

## Integration with the Image Processing Unit

The image processing unit, upon receiving both the image data and the corresponding image recognition support information from the image sensor, applies predetermined image processing operations to the image data. Critically, this processing is informed and enhanced by the support information provided by the sensor, rather than relying exclusively on raw pixel data analyzed from scratch.

By utilizing this pre-generated support information, the image processing unit can more efficiently identify regions of interest, prioritize computational resources, or streamline recognition algorithms, thereby substantially reducing the overall processing burden that would otherwise be required to perform equivalent recognition tasks using unprocessed image data alone. This division of labor between the sensor and the image processing unit represents an efficient architectural approach to distributing computational tasks across the imaging pipeline.

## Practical Applications

This technology finds particular applicability in imaging devices that incorporate recognition-based functionalities, with face detection representing a prominent example. In such applications—commonly found in digital cameras, smartphones, security systems, and other consumer or professional imaging devices—the ability to offload preliminary recognition-related computations to the image sensor itself can yield significant improvements in processing speed, power efficiency, and overall system responsiveness. This is especially valuable in scenarios requiring real-time face detection, such as autofocus systems, exposure adjustment based on facial regions, or immediate user feedback during image capture.

## Conclusion

By integrating area-based image recognition support information generation directly within the image sensor architecture, this disclosure presents a solution that meaningfully reduces the processing load traditionally imposed on image processing units. This approach not only enhances the efficiency of image recognition tasks but also enables more responsive and capable imaging devices, particularly those requiring sophisticated features like face detection, without necessitating proportional increases in processing hardware capability or power consumption.

# Imaging Apparatus, Image Sensor, and Image Processor with Region-Based Recognition Support

## Technical Field

The present disclosure relates to an imaging apparatus, an image sensor, and an image processor, and more particularly to technology for reducing the computational burden associated with image recognition processing by leveraging distributed, area-based analysis performed directly on the image sensor.

## Background

Modern imaging devices—including digital cameras, smartphones, surveillance systems, and various embedded vision systems—increasingly incorporate image recognition functionality such as face detection, object tracking, and scene classification. Conventionally, such recognition tasks are performed entirely by a downstream image processing unit or application processor after the full frame of image data has been read out from the image sensor. This approach requires the processor to analyze the entire captured image, often at high resolution, which imposes a substantial computational load. As image sensors continue to increase in resolution and frame rate, this processing burden grows correspondingly, leading to increased power consumption, processing latency, and hardware cost. There exists a need for a more efficient architecture that reduces the recognition-processing burden on the main image processing unit while maintaining or improving recognition accuracy and responsiveness.

## Summary of the Disclosure

To address the above-described problems, the present disclosure provides an imaging apparatus, an image sensor, and an image processor configured to distribute part of the image recognition workload to the image sensor itself, rather than relying solely on a downstream processing unit.

### Structural Overview

The imaging apparatus includes:

1. **An image sensor** having an imaging surface composed of a two-dimensional array of photoelectric conversion elements (pixels). The imaging surface is divided into a plurality of predetermined areas, each area comprising a subset of the photoelectric conversion elements.

2. **An area-based analysis unit** integrated into or closely coupled with the image sensor, configured to generate, for each divided area, "image recognition support information" based on the pixel signals output by the photoelectric conversion elements located within that particular area. This support information may include, without limitation, luminance statistics, contrast information, edge-detection results, motion vectors, color distribution data, or preliminary feature indicators relevant to recognition tasks such as face or object detection.

3. **An image processing unit** configured to receive both the image data (pixel signals) output from the image sensor and the corresponding image recognition support information generated on a per-area basis. The image processing unit applies predetermined image processing—such as region-of-interest extraction, exposure adjustment, noise reduction, or recognition algorithm execution—to the output image data, using the support information to guide, simplify, or accelerate the manner in which such processing is performed.

### Operational Principle

Rather than transmitting only the raw pixel data and requiring the image processing unit to perform full-frame analysis to identify areas of interest (e.g., regions likely containing a face), the image sensor itself performs a lightweight, localized analysis of each imaging-surface area concurrently with, or immediately following, signal readout. This localized analysis produces compact recognition support information corresponding to each area, which is transmitted alongside or embedded together with the image data.

The image processing unit then utilizes this support information to determine, for example, which areas are more likely to contain relevant recognition targets, thereby narrowing the scope of subsequent processing, adjusting processing parameters more efficiently, or bypassing full-frame scanning operations altogether. In this manner, computationally expensive operations, such as face detection, need not be performed uniformly and exhaustively across the entire image; instead, they can be selectively and adaptively directed to the areas indicated as relevant by the support information.

### Advantages

This area-based, sensor-assisted approach provides several benefits:

- **Reduced processing load**: Because preliminary analysis is distributed to the image sensor on a per-area basis, the image processing unit is relieved of performing exhaustive, full-resolution analysis, thereby lowering computational demand.

- **Improved processing speed**: Recognition-related operations such as face detection can be completed more quickly, since candidate areas are pre-identified or pre-characterized by the support information.

- **Lower power consumption**: Reduced computational load on the image processing unit translates into decreased power consumption, which is particularly advantageous for battery-operated or portable devices.

- **Scalability**: The area-based architecture is adaptable to sensors of varying resolution, since the number and size of divided areas can be configured according to processing requirements and available hardware resources.

- **Flexible application**: The generated support information can support multiple types of downstream image processing operations beyond face detection, including but not limited to autofocus assistance, automatic exposure control, white balance adjustment, and object tracking.

### Example Applications

The disclosed imaging apparatus, image sensor, and image processor are particularly well-suited for implementation in devices that require real-time or near-real-time image recognition capability under constrained processing resources. Representative applications include:

- Digital still cameras and video cameras equipped with face detection and autofocus functions
- Smartphones and tablet devices incorporating recognition-based camera features
- Surveillance and security cameras requiring efficient object or motion detection
- Automotive imaging systems for driver monitoring or object recognition
- Embedded and IoT vision devices with limited processing capability

### Detailed Description of Embodiments

In one embodiment, the imaging surface of the image sensor is divided into a grid of rectangular areas, each area containing a plurality of photoelectric conversion elements arranged in rows and columns. For each area, an on-chip or near-chip processing circuit calculates recognition support information such as average luminance, luminance variance, or simplified edge/gradient information based on the pixel signals within that area.

The image sensor outputs this recognition support information together with the corresponding pixel signal data, either as an integrated data stream or as separate but synchronized data channels, to the image processing unit.

The image processing unit, upon receiving the image data and the associated area-based recognition support information, performs predetermined image processing operations. For instance, in a face-detection application, the image processing unit may use the recognition support information to identify areas exhibiting characteristics consistent with skin tone, facial contours, or symmetrical feature patterns, and then apply a more detailed and computationally intensive face-detection algorithm only to those candidate areas rather than to the entire image frame.

In another embodiment, the recognition support information may be updated dynamically on a frame-by-frame basis, allowing the image processing unit to track changes across successive frames—such as movement of a detected face or object—without needing to reanalyze the entire image from scratch at each frame.

The division of the imaging surface into areas may be fixed in advance or may be configurable, allowing for adjustment of area size and shape according to the specific recognition task, sensor resolution, or processing requirements of the application.

### Conclusion

By having the image sensor itself divide the imaging surface into multiple areas and generate corresponding image recognition support information based on localized pixel signals, and by enabling the image processing unit to utilize this information to apply targeted and efficient image processing operations, the present disclosure achieves a significant reduction in the processing burden traditionally associated with image recognition tasks. This architecture enables faster, more power-efficient, and more scalable recognition processing, making it well-suited for a wide range of imaging devices, including cameras equipped with face detection and related recognition functions.

# The Word "The"

"The" is one of the most fundamental words in the English language, serving as the definite article. Despite being just three letters long, it holds the distinction of being the most frequently used word in English texts, appearing more often than any other word in written and spoken communication.

## Function and Purpose

The primary role of "the" is to specify particular nouns, distinguishing them from general or unspecified ones. When we say "the book" rather than "a book," we indicate that we're referring to a specific book already known to the listener or reader, perhaps mentioned earlier or understood from context. This contrasts with the indefinite articles "a" and "an," which introduce something new or unspecified.

## Historical Origins

The word "the" traces its roots back to Old English, evolving from the demonstrative pronoun "þe" (using the letter thorn, þ, which represented the "th" sound). Over centuries, it gradually transformed from a word that pointed to something specific into the article we use today.

## Linguistic Significance

Interestingly, not all languages have a direct equivalent to "the." Languages like Russian, Japanese, and Latin manage without definite articles altogether, relying on context and word order to convey similar meaning. This makes "the" a distinctive feature that language learners studying English often find challenging, as the rules governing when to use it—and when to omit it—can be surprisingly complex and filled with exceptions.

## Cultural Presence

Beyond grammar, "the" appears in countless idioms, titles, and phrases, cementing its place in everyday language. It often appears in band names, movie titles, and organizational names, sometimes fully capitalized for emphasis, as in "The Beatles" or "The New York Times," lending prominence to what follows.

In essence, this small word carries significant weight in shaping meaning, clarity, and specificity within the English language.

# Patent Abstract

**Imaging Apparatus with Area-Divided Recognition Support Information Generation**

An imaging apparatus is disclosed that reduces computational load on an image processing unit while maintaining image recognition accuracy. The apparatus includes an image sensor having a pixel array divided into a plurality of divided areas, each capable of independently capturing image data. The image sensor further includes a signal processing circuit configured to generate, for each divided area, recognition support information based on the captured image data of that respective area, prior to transmission to a downstream image processing unit.

The recognition support information may include feature quantities, luminance distribution data, motion vectors, region-of-interest indicators, or preliminary classification results extracted or computed on a per-divided-area basis at the sensor level. By performing this preliminary analysis at the pixel array or sensor chip level, rather than transferring raw image data for full-frame processing, the apparatus offloads a portion of the recognition-related computation from the image processing unit to the image sensor itself.

The image processing unit receives both the captured image data and the corresponding per-area recognition support information, and utilizes the support information to perform object recognition, region extraction, or subject tracking with reduced processing burden, since portions of the analysis have already been completed at the sensor stage. A control unit may selectively determine which divided areas require full image data transfer versus which require only recognition support information, based on scene conditions, motion detection, or region-of-interest determinations, further optimizing data transfer bandwidth and processing efficiency.

This configuration enables real-time or low-latency image recognition processing, reduced power consumption, and decreased data transmission bandwidth, making the apparatus particularly suitable for compact imaging devices, autonomous systems, surveillance cameras, and mobile devices requiring efficient on-device recognition capabilities.

# Technical Disclosure Summary

## Title
**Image Sensor System with Region-Based Recognition Support Data Output for Distributed Image Processing**

---

## Field of the Disclosure

This disclosure relates to image sensor architectures, and more particularly to an image sensor having a segmented imaging surface in which each segment independently generates recognition support data for consumption by a dedicated or shared downstream image processor.

---

## Background

Conventional image sensor systems capture raw pixel data across the entire imaging surface and transmit the complete frame to a single, centralized image signal processor (ISP) or application processor for subsequent tasks such as object detection, classification, tracking, and recognition. This monolithic approach presents several drawbacks:

1. **Bandwidth bottlenecks**: Full-frame transmission at high resolutions and frame rates consumes significant interconnect bandwidth (e.g., MIPI CSI lanes), particularly problematic in multi-camera or high-resolution systems.
2. **Latency**: Recognition tasks must wait for full-frame readout and transfer before processing can begin, increasing end-to-end latency for time-critical applications (e.g., autonomous driving, AR/VR, surveillance).
3. **Power consumption**: Transmitting and processing full raw frames when only certain regions contain features of interest wastes power.
4. **Processing bottleneck**: A single centralized processor must handle recognition workload for the entire frame, limiting scalability as sensor resolution increases.

There exists a need for an image sensor architecture that reduces data transmission overhead, lowers latency, and enables scalable, parallelized recognition processing by distributing preliminary recognition computation closer to the point of image capture.

---

## Summary of the Disclosure

The disclosed image sensor system divides the imaging surface into a plurality of discrete regions (tiles, blocks, or zones), each equipped with local analog and/or digital processing circuitry. Rather than (or in addition to) transmitting raw pixel data, each region computes and outputs **recognition support data** — a compact, region-specific representation extracted from the pixels within that region — which is used by one or more downstream image processors to perform or accelerate recognition tasks (e.g., object detection, feature matching, semantic segmentation, motion detection).

Each region's recognition support data is transmitted independently, and may be consumed by:
- A single centralized image processor that aggregates data from all regions, or
- Multiple dedicated image processors, each assigned to one or more regions, operating in parallel.

This architecture enables selective, prioritized, and parallelized processing, significantly reducing bandwidth and latency compared to full-frame transmission architectures.

---

## Detailed Description

### 1. Imaging Surface Segmentation

The imaging surface (pixel array) is partitioned into **N regions**, which may be:
- Fixed, uniform tiles (e.g., a grid of M×M blocks)
- Non-uniform regions defined by sensor geometry, optical characteristics (e.g., lens shading zones), or application-specific regions of interest (ROI)
- Dynamically reconfigurable regions, whose boundaries can be adjusted at runtime based on scene content, prior recognition results, or external control signals (e.g., from a host processor or previous frame's analysis)

Each region contains its own subset of the pixel array along with associated local processing logic, which may be implemented via:
- In-pixel or near-pixel analog processing circuits
- Per-region digital logic blocks (e.g., small ASIC/FPGA blocks integrated on the sensor die or in a stacked die configuration)
- Column-parallel or region-parallel readout and computation paths

### 2. Recognition Support Data Generation

For each region, local processing circuitry computes **recognition support data**, which may include one or more of:

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| **Feature descriptors** | Local gradient histograms (e.g., HOG-like features), edge maps, corner points, or keypoint descriptors extracted from the region |
| **Reduced-resolution/thumbnail data** | Downsampled or binned pixel data representing the region at lower fidelity |
| **Motion/change indicators** | Frame-to-frame difference metrics, motion vectors, or activity flags indicating temporal change within the region |
| **Confidence/saliency scores** | A scalar or low-dimensional vector indicating likelihood that the region contains an object of interest |
| **Compressed embeddings** | Output of a lightweight on-sensor neural network (e.g., a small CNN or binary neural network) producing a feature embedding vector |
| **Metadata tags** | Classification hints, bounding box proposals, or region-level labels derived from simplified on-sensor inference |

This recognition support data is significantly smaller in volume than raw pixel data for the region, enabling reduced-bandwidth transmission.

### 3. Region-to-Processor Mapping

The system architecture supports flexible mapping between imaging regions and downstream image processors:

- **One-to-one mapping**: Each region is paired with a dedicated image processor (e.g., a small embedded core or accelerator), enabling fully parallel recognition pipelines.
- **Many-to-one mapping**: Multiple regions feed into a shared image processor, which aggregates recognition support data to perform frame-level or multi-region recognition (e.g., stitching partial detections across region boundaries).
- **Dynamic/reconfigurable mapping**: A control layer (on-sensor or off-sensor) dynamically assigns regions to available processors based on current workload, detected activity, or power/performance targets.

### 4. Data Output and Interface

Recognition support data from each region is transmitted via:
- Independent output channels/lanes per region (e.g., separate virtual channels within a MIPI CSI-2 interface), allowing parallel, low-latency delivery
- A time-multiplexed shared bus with region-tagged packets
- Optional raw pixel data transmission for select regions (e.g., regions flagged as high-interest) alongside recognition support data for all other regions, enabling a hybrid full-resolution/summary approach

Each output packet includes a **region identifier**, **timestamp/frame index**, and the recognition support payload, allowing downstream processors to correctly associate and, if needed, re-assemble region-level results into a frame-level understanding.

### 5. Downstream Processing

Each image processor receiving recognition support data performs recognition-related computation using this data instead of (or in addition to) raw pixels:

- Processors may execute lightweight inference (e.g., classification confirmation, tracking updates) using the received feature data directly, avoiding redundant re-extraction of features from raw pixels.
- In multi-processor configurations, a coordinating processor or software layer aggregates partial results (e.g., bounding boxes, embeddings) from multiple region-based processors to produce a final scene-level recognition output (e.g., full-frame object list, tracked identities).
- Feedback signals from image processors may be routed back to the sensor to dynamically adjust region boundaries, resolution, frame rate, or recognition support data type on a per-region basis for subsequent frames (closed-loop optimization).

---

## Example System Architecture

```
                     Imaging Surface (Pixel Array)
    ┌───────────┬───────────┬───────────┬───────────┐
    │ Region 1  │ Region 2  │ Region 3  │ Region 4  │
    │ + Local   │ + Local   │ + Local   │ + Local   │
    │ Processing│ Processing│ Processing│ Processing│
    └─────┬─────┴─────┬─────┴─────┬─────┴─────┬─────┘
          │           │           │           │
   Recognition   Recognition Recognition Recognition
   Support Data  Support Data Support Data Support Data
          │           │           │           │
          ▼           ▼           ▼           ▼
   ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐ ┌───────────┐
   │ Image     │ │ Image     │ │ Image     │ │ Image     │
   │ Processor │ │ Processor │ │ Processor │ │ Processor │
   │    A      │ │    B      │ │    C      │ │    D      │
   └─────┬─────┘ └─────┬─────┘ └─────┬─────┘ └─────┬─────┘
         └─────────────┴─────────────┴─────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
                Aggregation / Fusion Layer
                          │
                          ▼
                Final Recognition Output
```

*(Alternative configuration: all four region outputs feed a single centralized processor.)*

---

## Advantages

1. **Reduced bandwidth**: Compact recognition support data replaces or supplements full raw-frame transfer, easing interconnect and memory bandwidth requirements.
2. **Lower latency**: Region-level data can be generated and transmitted as soon as that region's readout completes, without waiting for the full frame, and processing can begin immediately downstream.
3. **Scalability**: Additional regions and processors can be added to scale system throughput without a proportional increase in centralized processing burden.
4. **Power efficiency**: Regions without relevant content can transmit minimal data (e.g., a "no activity" flag) rather than full pixel data, reducing overall power draw.
5. **Flexible deployment**: Supports both centralized and distributed processing topologies within the same sensor design, adaptable to different system-level requirements (e.g., cost-sensitive vs. performance-sensitive applications).
6. **Improved recognition accuracy through specialization**: Dedicated per-region processors can be tuned or specialized for expected content characteristics of that region (e.g., sky detection in upper regions of an automotive camera, road-surface analysis in lower regions).

---

## Alternative Embodiments

- **Stacked sensor architecture**: The recognition support data generation circuitry resides on a separate logic die stacked with the pixel die (e.g., via hybrid bonding), with per-region processing blocks aligned to corresponding pixel array regions.
- **Hierarchical regions**: Regions may be further subdivided into sub-regions with a hierarchical recognition support data structure (e.g., coarse region-level saliency plus fine sub-region feature descriptors), enabling multi-resolution recognition pipelines.
- **Adaptive region sizing**: Region boundaries and sizes are dynamically adjusted frame-to-frame based on prior recognition results, effectively implementing an attention mechanism at the sensor level.
- **Hybrid raw/support data output**: The sensor selectively transmits full raw pixel data only for regions where recognition support data indicates high likelihood of an object of interest, while transmitting only recognition support data for all other regions, optimizing overall bandwidth use.
- **Multi-sensor systems**: In multi-camera systems, regions may span across sensors, with cross-sensor recognition support data aggregation performed by a shared processing layer.

---

## Potential Applications

- Automotive ADAS/autonomous driving perception systems
- Surveillance and security camera systems with edge-based analytics
- AR/VR headset cameras requiring low-latency object/hand/eye tracking
- Industrial machine vision systems with region-specific inspection requirements
- Multi-camera robotics and drone vision systems

# PATENT SPECIFICATION

## TITLE OF THE INVENTION

**IMAGING APPARATUS, IMAGE SENSOR, AND IMAGE PROCESSOR FOR REGION-BASED PRE-PROCESSING OF PIXEL SIGNALS TO REDUCE IMAGE RECOGNITION PROCESSING BURDEN**

---

## TECHNICAL FIELD

[0001] The present invention relates to an imaging apparatus, an image sensor, and an image processor, and more particularly to a technique for reducing the computational burden imposed on downstream image recognition processing by performing pre-processing of pixel signals on a region-by-region basis at the image sensor stage, prior to output of image data to a subsequent recognition-processing unit.

---

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

[0002] In recent years, imaging apparatuses incorporating image recognition functionality have been widely deployed in fields such as onboard vehicle systems, surveillance systems, robotics, and mobile terminals. In such apparatuses, an image sensor captures an image of a subject, and a downstream image recognition processing unit performs recognition processing, such as object detection, face detection, or feature-point extraction, upon the captured image data.

[0003] However, in a conventional configuration, the image sensor merely outputs raw pixel signals, or pixel signals subjected only to rudimentary correction such as defect correction or gain adjustment, for substantially the entirety of the imaging region. Consequently, the image recognition processing unit is compelled to execute recognition processing computations uniformly across the entire image, including image regions that are of low relevance or no relevance to the recognition target. This gives rise to several disadvantages.

[0004] First, the computational load imposed upon the image recognition processing unit becomes excessive, requiring a processor of high processing capability, which in turn increases apparatus cost and power consumption. Second, since recognition processing is performed uniformly regardless of the actual distribution of image content, processing time is elongated, and recognition results are delayed, which is particularly disadvantageous in applications requiring real-time responsiveness, such as vehicle collision avoidance systems. Third, when the imaging apparatus is a battery-driven mobile device, the increased computational burden shortens battery life significantly.

[0005] Various techniques have been proposed to address such problems, including reducing image resolution prior to recognition processing, or restricting recognition processing to a region of interest determined by a separate sensor. However, in the former case, a reduction in resolution across the entire image degrades recognition accuracy uniformly, including in regions where high resolution is actually necessary for accurate recognition. In the latter case, an additional sensor or mechanism for determining the region of interest is required, which increases the size and the cost of the apparatus.

[0006] Accordingly, there exists a need in the art for an imaging apparatus, an image sensor, and an image processor capable of reducing the computational burden of image recognition processing without necessitating additional external sensing components, and without uniformly degrading image quality across the entire captured image.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

[0007] The present invention has been made in view of the above-described problems, and an object of the present invention is to provide an imaging apparatus, an image sensor, and an image processor capable of reducing the processing burden imposed upon image recognition processing by performing pre-processing of pixel signals, on a region-by-region basis, at a stage prior to transfer of the pixel signals to an external image recognition processing unit.

[0008] In order to achieve the above object, according to one aspect of the present invention, there is provided an image sensor comprising: a pixel array section including a plurality of pixels arranged in a matrix, the pixel array section being logically divided into a plurality of regions; a signal generating section configured to generate pixel signals corresponding to light incident upon the plurality of pixels; a region-based pre-processing section configured to perform, for each of the plurality of regions independently, a pre-processing operation upon the pixel signals belonging to the corresponding region, the pre-processing operation including at least one of a region importance determination operation, a region-specific signal correction operation, a region-specific compression operation, and a region-specific feature extraction operation; and an output section configured to output, to an external processing unit, pre-processed pixel signals together with region-attribute information indicating a result of the pre-processing operation performed for each region.

[0009] According to another aspect of the present invention, there is provided an imaging apparatus comprising the above-described image sensor, an optical system configured to focus incident light onto the pixel array section of the image sensor, and an image recognition processing unit configured to perform image recognition processing upon the pre-processed pixel signals output from the image sensor, based on the region-attribute information.

[0010] According to yet another aspect of the present invention, there is provided an image processor comprising: an input section configured to receive, from an image sensor, pixel signals that have been pre-processed on a region-by-region basis and region-attribute information corresponding thereto; a region selecting section configured to select, based on the region-attribute information, at least one region among the plurality of regions as a processing-target region for image recognition processing; and a recognition processing section configured to execute the image recognition processing preferentially, or exclusively, with respect to the pixel signals corresponding to the processing-target region selected by the region selecting section.

[0011] By virtue of the above-described configuration, since the pre-processing of the pixel signals, including determination of the relative importance of each region for purposes of image recognition, is performed on the image sensor itself prior to the output of the pixel signals, the downstream image recognition processing unit is relieved of the necessity of performing full-scale recognition processing computations uniformly over the entire captured image. As a result, the processing burden, processing time, and power consumption of the image recognition processing unit can be significantly reduced, without necessitating additional external sensors, and without uniformly degrading the image quality of the entire captured image.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE PREFERRED EMBODIMENTS

### 1. Overall Configuration of the Imaging Apparatus

[0013] FIG. 1 is a block diagram showing a schematic configuration of an imaging apparatus 1 according to an embodiment of the present invention. As illustrated in FIG. 1, the imaging apparatus 1 includes an optical system 10, an image sensor 100, an image processor 200, a memory 300, and a control unit 400.

[0014] The optical system 10 includes one or more lenses, and is configured to focus incident light from a subject onto a pixel array section 110 of the image sensor 100. The image sensor 100 photoelectrically converts the incident light to generate pixel signals, performs region-based pre-processing upon the pixel signals as described in detail below, and outputs pre-processed pixel signals together with region-attribute information to the image processor 200.

[0015] The image processor 200 receives the pre-processed pixel signals and the region-attribute information from the image sensor 100, selects one or more processing-target regions based on the region-attribute information, and executes image recognition processing preferentially, or exclusively, with respect to the selected processing-target regions. The memory 300 stores the pre-processed pixel signals, the region-attribute information, and recognition results, among other data. The control unit 400 controls the overall operation of the imaging apparatus 1, including the operation timing of the image sensor 100 and the image processor 200.

[0016] It is to be understood that the image sensor 100 and the image processor 200 may be implemented as a single semiconductor chip in a stacked configuration, or as separate semiconductor chips connected via a suitable interface, without departing from the scope of the present invention.

### 2. Configuration of the Image Sensor

[0017] FIG. 2 is a block diagram showing a schematic configuration of the image sensor 100. As illustrated in FIG. 2, the image sensor 100 includes a pixel array section 110, a signal generating section 120, a region dividing section 130, a region-based pre-processing section 140, and an output section 150.

[0018] The pixel array section 110 includes a plurality of pixels arranged in a matrix along a row direction and a column direction, each pixel including a photoelectric conversion element, such as a photodiode, configured to generate an electric charge corresponding to an amount of incident light.

[0019] The signal generating section 120 is configured to read out the electric charge accumulated in each pixel of the pixel array section 110 and to generate a corresponding pixel signal, for example, by way of a column-parallel analog-to-digital converter or the like.

[0020] The region dividing section 130 logically divides the pixel array section 110 into a plurality of regions R1, R2, ..., Rn, as illustrated in FIG. 3. Each region may correspond, for example, to a rectangular block comprised of a predetermined number of rows and columns of pixels, although the shape and size of each region are not limited thereto, and may be set variably in accordance with an imaging mode, a recognition target, or a preceding recognition result.

[0021] The region-based pre-processing section 140 performs, for each of the plurality of regions independently, a pre-processing operation upon the pixel signals belonging to the corresponding region. In the present embodiment, the region-based pre-processing section 140 includes a region importance determination unit 141, a signal correction unit 142, a compression unit 143, and a feature extraction unit 144.

[0022] The region importance determination unit 141 is configured to calculate, for each region, an importance level indicating a degree of relevance of the region to image recognition processing. The importance level may be calculated, for example, based on at least one of: a luminance variance within the region; an edge amount, or contrast level, detected within the region; a motion amount detected between the current frame and a preceding frame within the region; and a preceding recognition result indicating that an object was previously detected within, or in the vicinity of, the region.

[0023] The signal correction unit 142 is configured to perform, for each region, a signal correction operation, which may include at least one of noise reduction, gain adjustment, white balance adjustment, and dynamic range adjustment, wherein a parameter of the signal correction operation is set individually for each region in accordance with the importance level calculated by the region importance determination unit 141. For example, a region having a relatively high importance level may be subjected to a correction operation with a higher noise-reduction strength, or a higher effective bit depth, than a region having a relatively low importance level.

[0024] The compression unit 143 is configured to perform, for each region, a compression operation upon the pixel signals, wherein a compression ratio is set individually for each region in accordance with the importance level. For example, a region having a relatively low importance level may be compressed at a relatively high compression ratio, or may be subjected to resolution reduction by pixel-signal thinning or pixel-signal addition, whereas a region having a relatively high importance level may be output at, or near, full resolution without substantial compression.

# SUMMARY

Disclosed herein are systems, devices, and methods relating to an image sensor architecture configured to perform localized, zone-based computation of recognition-support metadata prior to, or concurrently with, full-frame image processing by a downstream image signal processor (ISP) or host processing system.

In one aspect, an imaging apparatus is provided comprising a pixel array configured to capture image data corresponding to a scene, and an on-sensor processing circuit integrated with, or disposed in close proximity to, the pixel array. The on-sensor processing circuit is configured to partition the captured image data into a plurality of zones, each zone corresponding to a spatial region of the pixel array smaller than the full frame. For at least a subset of the plurality of zones, the on-sensor processing circuit computes one or more recognition-support metadata values indicative of a likelihood that the zone contains a face or other object of interest, and/or characteristics useful for subsequent face detection, face recognition, tracking, or related computer vision operations. Such metadata may include, without limitation, indicators of edge density, feature point locations, luminance and contrast statistics, candidate facial landmark positions, coarse orientation or pose estimates, skin-tone probability values, motion vectors, region-of-interest confidence scores, or partial feature descriptors suitable for downstream classification.

In some embodiments, the on-sensor processing circuit performs the zone-based metadata computation using dedicated hardware logic co-located with the pixel array or column/row readout circuitry, such that the metadata is generated in a pipelined or line-by-line manner substantially concurrently with image readout, rather than requiring the full frame to be first transferred to an external processor. This enables early identification of zones likely to contain faces, allowing the imaging apparatus or a downstream system to selectively prioritize, allocate additional processing resources to, adjust capture parameters for, or trigger full-resolution readout of only those zones, thereby reducing overall latency, memory bandwidth, and power consumption associated with face detection and recognition tasks.

In further embodiments, the recognition-support metadata generated for each zone is packaged together with, or in association with, the corresponding image data and transmitted to a downstream processing entity, such as an ISP, application processor, or neural network accelerator, which utilizes the metadata to guide, constrain, or accelerate subsequent full-image face detection, face recognition, exposure control, autofocus, or other computational photography operations. In some implementations, the metadata may be used to dynamically adjust sensor operating parameters, such as zone-specific gain, exposure time, or readout rate, prior to or during capture of a subsequent frame.

Also disclosed are corresponding methods of operating an image sensor to generate zone-based recognition-support metadata, methods of utilizing such metadata in downstream image processing pipelines, and camera systems, mobile devices, and other apparatuses incorporating the disclosed image sensor architecture. The disclosed embodiments provide improvements in processing efficiency, latency reduction, and power consumption relative to conventional systems in which face detection and recognition are performed exclusively after full-frame image transfer and reconstruction.

counterfactuals.output:
# ABSTRACT

An imaging apparatus includes an imaging element having a plurality of photoelectric conversion elements arranged on an imaging surface, the imaging surface being divided into a plurality of areas. Each of the plurality of areas includes a subset of the photoelectric conversion elements configured to generate image data based on light incident thereon. A processing unit is operatively coupled to the imaging element and is configured to generate, for each of the plurality of areas, recognition support information based on the image data generated by the photoelectric conversion elements included in the respective area. The recognition support information generated for each area is output in association with a position of the corresponding area on the imaging surface, such that the recognition support information can be utilized by a downstream image processing apparatus to assist in a recognition processing performed on the image data. By generating the recognition support information on a per-area basis at the imaging element or an associated processing circuit prior to output, a processing load imposed on the downstream image processing apparatus for performing the recognition processing is reduced, thereby enabling faster and more efficient recognition processing while maintaining reduced power consumption and circuit scale in the overall imaging system. The recognition support information may include, for example, feature amount data, brightness information, contrast information, edge information, motion information, or object detection information corresponding to the image data of each area, and may be selectively generated or updated based on an imaging condition, a recognition target, or a control signal received from the downstream image processing apparatus, thereby allowing flexible allocation of recognition-related processing between the imaging apparatus and the downstream image processing apparatus.
